newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bread-maker fined for price fixing.
newsitem.headline: Australian bread-maker fined for price fixing.

text.p: Australia's largest bread-making group, George Weston Foods Ltd, has been fined A$1.25 million (US$950,000) by the Australia's Federal Court for price fixing, Australia's anti-monopoly watchdog said on Friday.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commision (ACCC) said George Weston, trading as Tip Top Bakeries, admitted having stopped supplying retailers because the retailers were discounting the price of bread.
The incidents occurred at Ferntree Gully in Victoria and at Albury in New South Wales in November 1995, the ACCC said.

George Weston, 78 percent owned by Associated British Foods Plc, had also admitted agreeing to a demand by the Woolworths Ltd owned retailer, Safeway Stores, to increase the price at which a Tip Top retail store would sell bread to the public.
"The company (George Weston) admitted the contraventions and has substantially assisted the ACCC with its investigation from an early stage," the ACCC said.
George Weston's offences arose out of pressure from Safeway, but that Safeway had denied the allegations, the ACCC said.
The Federal Court said in its judgment against George Weston it had taken into account Tip Top's relatively high public profile in deciding the penalty.
ACCC Chairman Allan Fels said the commission was concerned whenever wholesalers or manufacturers try to manipulate prices.
"The ACCC is concerned whenever manufacturers, or wholesalers, try to manipulate retail prices or decide who will, or will not, be able to act competitively," Fels said in a statement.

"This is a case where the rights of small businesses, who were attempting to compete with larger supermarkets, were ignored for the purposes of preserving Tip Top's relationship with larger customers," he said.
"The ACCC will have no hesitation in taking appropriate action should similar circumstances occur in the future."
The ACCC said it continued to pursue its allegations against Safeway and two of its employees involved in the George Weston incidents and in other incidents involving other bread-makers.
Safeway denied the allegations and a trial was expected within the next six to eight weeks.
An ACCC spokeswoman could not say who the other bread-makers involved were. The ACCC was not prosecuting Safeway's parent, Woolworths, or any of the other bread-makers, she said.
Industry sources said Australia's second largest bread-maker Goodman Fielder Ltd had also been approached by Safeway to fix prices and stop supplying smaller independent retailers.
George Weston has 32 percent of the Australian bread market while Goodman Fielder has 28 percent.

"Franklins and Davids are causing the major retailers a lot pain and these big retailers like Woolworths and Coles Myer are hitting back in a fairly aggressive way and suppliers get caught in the middle," one source said.
"What Safeway and George Weston was doing was pretty blunt, but there are other legal ways of applying such pressure," another source said.
